stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Linguists have often assumed that speakers of tonal languages lose their tonal distinctions when they whisper, since whispering removes the vocal-fold vibration that produces pitch. A study led by phonetician Mara Odili complicates that view. Odili recorded speakers whispering pairs of words that differ only in tone, and listeners still identified the intended word about 80 percent of the time. Speakers, it seems, lean on other cues, such as vowel length and loudness, to carry the contrast when pitch is unavailable.
choices: To challenge an assumption about what happens to tonal contrasts in whispered speech
To describe a method for recording whispered word pairs in a tonal language
To argue that pitch plays no real role in distinguishing words in tonal languages
To explain why listeners struggle to understand whispered words in tonal languages
explanation: The text opens with what linguists 'have often assumed' and then says Odili's study 'complicates that view.' Everything after that is evidence that whispered tones still come through. So the text exists to challenge the assumption, and the study is the evidence it uses.

B.why: You picked what the text contains (a recording study) instead of what it is for. The study is evidence against the assumption. The text says almost nothing about method.

C.why: You pushed the finding too far. The text says speakers use other cues when pitch is unavailable. It never says pitch doesn't matter in ordinary speech.

D.why: You reversed the finding. Listeners identified the intended word about 80 percent of the time, so the text shows they mostly succeed, not that they struggle.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Folklorists have long traced the dozens of Baltic versions of "The Miller and the Three Geese" to a single printed anthology from 1812, assuming that villagers learned the tale from that book. Folklorist Ines Varga questions this account. In tellings she gathered from remote farming communities, the geese have names and the miller is a woman. Neither detail appears in the anthology, but both appear in a sermon manuscript from 1740. Varga concludes that the tale was circulating orally well before the anthology was printed.
choices: To present details from village tellings of a tale that differ from its printed version
To challenge a widely held explanation of how a tale became known in a region
To argue that printed anthologies had no influence on Baltic folk tales
To show that the 1812 anthology copied its version of the tale from a 1740 sermon
explanation: The first sentence gives the long-held belief that the tale spread from an 1812 book. Then 'Varga questions this account,' and the details from the village tellings and the sermon are her evidence that the tale was told aloud before the book existed. The text's purpose is to challenge that explanation of how the tale spread.

A.why: You described the evidence instead of the point it supports. The village details matter only because they undercut the belief that the tale came from the anthology.

C.why: You turned a narrow claim into a sweeping one. Varga argues only that this tale was told orally before 1812. She says nothing about anthologies having no influence at all.

D.why: You missed the key contrast. The named geese and the woman miller are absent from the anthology, so the text gives no sign that the anthology copied the sermon.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Because sea cucumbers have no eyes, researchers have generally assumed that the animals cannot respond to light. Marine biologist Teodor Haas found otherwise. When he passed a shadow over individuals of one shallow-water species, they contracted their bodies within seconds, a common defensive reaction. Haas suspects that light-sensitive cells scattered across the skin are responsible. He cautions that he tested only a single species, but he argues that lacking eyes need not mean lacking any ability to detect light.
choices: To describe how one sea cucumber species reacts when a shadow passes over it
To explain why Haas doubts that sea cucumbers are able to respond to light
To question the belief that lacking eyes leaves sea cucumbers unable to sense light
To argue that sea cucumbers detect light as effectively as animals with eyes
explanation: The text starts with what researchers 'have generally assumed' (no eyes means no response to light) and then turns with 'Haas found otherwise.' The shadow experiment is evidence against that assumption, and Haas's closing point states the challenge directly. The text's purpose is to question the belief.

A.why: You chose the part that takes up the most space, the shadow experiment, rather than the job it does. It is evidence used to question an assumption, not the text's main purpose.

B.why: You got Haas's position backward. He found that sea cucumbers do respond to light. The doubt belongs to the earlier researchers he is challenging.

D.why: You overstated the finding. Haas shows only that one species reacts to a shadow, and he warns that he tested a single species. Nothing compares how well sea cucumbers and animals with eyes detect light.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Farmers have traditionally treated earthworms as a simple sign of healthy soil: the more worms, the better the field. Soil scientist Rafael Okonjo's survey of forty wheat plots complicates that rule of thumb. Plots with the most worms did absorb rainwater faster, but they also lost more nitrogen, as worm burrows carried dissolved fertilizer below the root zone. Abundant worms, Okonjo concludes, signal some benefits but not uniformly healthier soil.
choices: To report survey findings on how quickly rainwater soaked into forty wheat plots
To show that earthworms harm wheat fields more than they benefit those fields
To argue that worm burrows keep dissolved fertilizer from sinking below the roots
To complicate the common view that more earthworms always means healthier soil
explanation: The first sentence states a traditional belief: more worms means better soil. The second says the survey 'complicates that rule of thumb'. The mixed results (faster absorption but more nitrogen loss) are the evidence. The text's purpose is to complicate the belief, not to reverse it.

A.why: You picked one detail from the survey. Water absorption is only half the evidence, and the evidence serves to question a traditional belief.

B.why: You turned 'not uniformly healthier' into 'more harm than benefit'. The text grants real benefits and never weighs them against the costs.

C.why: You reversed the finding. The burrows carried fertilizer below the root zone. They did not keep it out.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Some linguists suggest that languages with many speakers tend to have simpler grammar, since large numbers of adult learners smooth away irregular forms. A comparison of sixty languages by Hana Lindqvist offers partial support but urges caution: although the overall trend held, several widely spoken languages kept highly irregular verb systems, and some small languages had very regular ones. Population size, Lindqvist argues, may be one influence on grammar among many, not a reliable predictor.
choices: To caution against treating population size as a dependable predictor of simple grammar
To refute the claim that population size has any connection to grammatical complexity
To describe the sample of sixty languages that were compared in Lindqvist's study
To explain how adult learners make the grammar of small languages more irregular
explanation: The text begins with what 'some linguists suggest' and then 'urges caution'. The exceptions are the evidence. The last sentence keeps population size as 'one influence' but rejects it as 'a reliable predictor'. That is a warning against overstating the idea, not a rejection of it.

B.why: You fell for the harder version of the trap. The text says the overall trend held, so population size still matters. It warns against overstating the link but does not refute it.

C.why: You named what the text contains, a study, rather than what it does. The comparison is evidence for a caution about an existing claim.

D.why: You mixed up the mechanism. According to the text, adult learners smooth away irregular forms. They don't add them, and the claim is about large languages, not small ones.

C.why: You missed the qualifier. The last sentence says wider cracks still had to be repaired, so the text does not claim repair is unnecessary.

D.why: You reversed the result. Only gaps up to 0.5 millimeters filled, and wider cracks still needed repair.

To argue that upland wetlands raise flood peaks and should no longer be protected

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Forecasters have often treated a towering cloud top as the clearest warning that a thunderstorm will produce hail. A review of radar records from 1,200 storms suggests that this signal deserves less weight. Cloud height is not irrelevant: short storms with no rotation rarely produced hail. To argue that cloud height has no connection at all to whether a thunderstorm will produce hail

The comparison supports that doubt: shorter rotating storms produced hail 41 percent of the time, almost twice the 22 percent rate for tall storms without rotation. The author also says height is 'not irrelevant,' so the purpose is to question how much forecasters rely on height, not to throw it out.

B.why: You missed the qualifier. The author says cloud height is 'not irrelevant,' because short storms without rotation rarely made hail. The text warns against overrating height. It doesn't reject height altogether.

C.why: You summarized the data instead of naming its job. The percentages are evidence for the claim that cloud height deserves less weight. Reporting them is not the purpose of the text.

D.why: You reversed the author's position. The radar review shows that rotation predicted hail better than height did, so the forecasters' assumption is being questioned, not confirmed.
